text: Cherokee County has a moratorium in force on approving the use of county roads, resources or infrastructure for commercial wind, solar and battery storage projects, among other uses, with a ban on building them in the unincorporated county during its term. The county adopted it on December 22, 2025 and re-adopted it on June 8, 2026.

A county resolution adopted October 3, 2022 regulates industrial-scale wind turbines with a 5,250-foot setback from the nearest property line, a 440-foot height limit and a 39 dBA noise limit from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m.
Kansas leaves wind and solar siting to cities and counties through planning and zoning, and no state body sites these projects. Neither utilities nor developers may condemn land for these facilities.
Clearway Energy's proposed Rainbow Springs Solar project is on record as pending since December 2025.
The moratorium runs through March 31, 2027.
One contested project is on record: Clearway Energy's proposed Rainbow Springs Solar project, pending since December 2025.

Two county rules are on record and in force, both checked against the instruments themselves: a moratorium on commercial renewable energy, battery storage and other uses, through March 31, 2027, and an October 3, 2022 wind resolution with a 5,250-foot setback, a 440-foot height limit and an overnight 39 dBA noise limit.

Kansas leaves wind and solar siting to cities and counties through planning and zoning, and no state body sites these projects. State law also bars utilities and developers from condemning land for them.

Two one-year moratoria are in force in Nicholas County: the fiscal court adopted one on wind energy projects of any size on August 14, 2026, and one on the solar systems its 2024 solar ordinance covers on September 18, 2026.

The county's solar ordinance, passed 6-0 on June 14, 2024, requires a county license for intermediate-scale and large-scale ground-mounted solar and sets the solar footprint at least 2,000 feet from any non-participating property line and any public road or rail right-of-way.

Under Kentucky law, a merchant plant of 10 MW or more needs a certificate from the state siting board, and local planning and zoning setbacks prevail over a conflicting board order. On May 29, 2026 the Kentucky Court of Appeals held that only a planning and zoning commission may adopt such rules, and that ruling is not final.

South Fork Solar, Heelstone Energy's large-scale solar project on Carpenter Pike, is pending. The fiscal court voted unanimously to uphold its 2024 ordinance against Heelstone's request for an amendment, and passed the solar moratorium 5-1 on September 18, 2026.
The wind moratorium runs to August 14, 2027, and the solar moratorium runs to September 18, 2027.

One contested project is on record: South Fork Solar, a large-scale solar project on Carpenter Pike, is pending. The fiscal court upheld its 2024 solar ordinance against the developer's amendment request and adopted a one-year solar moratorium 5-1 on September 18, 2026.

Three county rules are on record and in force, all checked against the instruments themselves: the June 2024 solar ordinance with its 2,000-foot setback, and one-year moratoria on wind (August 14, 2026) and on solar (September 18, 2026).

The state siting board certifies merchant plants of 10 MW or more, with wind turbines at least 1,000 feet from property lines and all plants 2,000 feet from residential neighborhoods, schools, hospitals and nursing homes. Local zoning setbacks prevail where adopted, and a May 29, 2026 Court of Appeals ruling, not yet final, limits them to planning and zoning commissions.

Two Town of Concord moratoria are in force, one on battery energy storage and one on solar, and they apply only in Concord. The town board extended both for six months on June 11, 2026, the storage moratorium to about December 2026.

New York's Office of Renewable Energy Siting and Electric Transmission (ORES) permits renewable facilities of 25 MW or more and may decline to apply a local law it finds unreasonably burdensome. Smaller facilities stay under municipal land use control, and stand-alone battery storage is outside the ORES rules.

Boston's town board extended its battery storage moratorium on December 3, 2025. In Aurora and Eden, the record's end dates for their battery storage moratoria (June 9, 2026 and September 30, 2026) have passed, and no later extension is on record. The Boston and Aurora records are not yet checked against the instruments themselves.

As compiled by NREL, the Town of Tonawanda's wind ordinance includes a ban, and Orchard Park's solar ordinance and Aurora's wind ordinance include a zoning prohibition. These records apply in those towns only and are not yet checked against the instruments themselves.

Two Concord moratoria are in force in that town, Boston extended its storage moratorium on December 3, 2025, and the Aurora and Eden end dates have passed with no later extension on record. NREL compiled solar or wind ordinances for many towns and Buffalo, and these and the Boston and Aurora records are not yet checked against the instruments.

The state siting office (ORES) permits renewable facilities of 25 MW or more under uniform state setbacks, such as 250 feet from non-participating homes for solar, and may set aside local laws it finds unreasonably burdensome. Smaller facilities stay under municipal land use control, and stand-alone battery storage is outside the ORES rules.
